about: One line back after each answer on the free check (Rory's review: each answer should teach something). These are GridSchool's read, shown under the label 'Our read', not statistics. Add a number only with a dated source.

stage.grad: New grads are judged mostly on what a stranger can open and check: a project, a repo, a write-up.
stage.self: Without a degree to lean on, the first thing a reviewer can open does most of the work.
stage.working: Working engineers are hired through people more often than portals. We'll see how much of your search goes that way.
stage.laidoff: A gap is easier to explain than most people fear. What matters is what you did with it.

role.fullstack: Full-stack means different things at each company. Saying which half you lead with helps you get read.
role.backend: Backend reviewers look for systems you ran and what broke, more than the languages you list.
role.ai: Applied AI teams want proof you can check what a model did, not only that you can call one.
role.frontend: Frontend work is the easiest to show. A link a reviewer can open beats any bullet.
role.platform: Platform teams hire on what you kept running, and how you handled it when it didn't.
role.unsure: That's common. One target for the next month usually gets more replies than keeping every door open.

level.entry: At entry level, reviewers look for one thing you built and can explain end to end.
level.mid: Mid level is where owning something from start to finish starts to matter.
level.senior: Senior roles are read for scope: what you decided, not only what you built.
level.staff: Staff roles are mostly filled through people who already know your work.

months.lt1: Early is the best time to fix where your applications land.
months.1to3: A month or two in is when the pattern in your replies starts to show.
months.3to6: After a few months, changing the channel usually helps more than sending more.
months.6to12: After this long, changing the channel usually helps more than sending more.
months.gt12: After this long, it's rarely effort. It's usually where the effort goes.

apps.none: Good. You can aim before you send.
apps.1to20: That's enough to learn from. What came back tells us where it's stuck.
apps.21to75: At this volume, silence usually points at where they land, not at you.
apps.76to200: At this volume, silence usually points at where they land, not at you.
apps.gt200: At this volume, silence usually points at where they land, not at you.

stop.replies: Silence at this stage usually comes from the resume or the channel. Both are fixable.
stop.screen: Getting the call means your resume works. What you say on the call is the next thing to look at.
stop.technical: Reaching the technical round means you're getting through. Practice on that format is the lever.
stop.final: Final-round no's are often about the story and fit more than skill.
stop.offers: Offers mean you're hireable. The fix is where you aim.
